subject: Embedding space fragmentation under continual adapter-based fine-tuning without rehearsal across sequentially introduced task distributions

Topic: Embedding space fragmentation under continual adapter-based fine-tuning without rehearsal across sequentially introduced task distributions

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1534)
response:
The central question is whether adapter modules — small trainable bottleneck layers inserted into a frozen pretrained backbone — can be added sequentially for new tasks without corrupting the geometric structure of the representation space that earlier tasks depend on. The key concepts in play are: (1) adapter-based fine-tuning, where only a small parameter subset is trained while the backbone is frozen, ostensibly protecting prior knowledge; (2) continual learning without rehearsal, meaning no examples from previous tasks are retained or replayed during new training; and (3) embedding space fragmentation, the phenomenon where the internal geometry — distances, cluster separability, manifold structure — degrades across task boundaries even when raw accuracy on held-out benchmarks appears stable. The beginner assumes that freezing the backbone is sufficient protection, reasoning that if backbone weights don't change, representations can't drift. What the expert worries about is subtler: adapter outputs are injected back into the residual stream, so each new adapter reshapes the effective transformation the frozen layers produce, and the composition of sequentially trained adapters can induce interference patterns that distort inter-class and inter-task geometric relationships without touching a single backbone weight. The practical consequence is that downstream components relying on embedding geometry — retrieval systems, linear probes, similarity-based classifiers — can silently degrade across tasks even as task-specific classification heads maintain their nominal accuracy, making the failure mode invisible to standard evaluation protocols.

NEXT: If the backbone weights are truly frozen, what specific mechanism inside the residual stream allows a new adapter, trained only on task N, to alter the effective representations seen by task N-1's adapter?

The residual stream in a transformer is an additive channel: each layer computes a delta and adds it directly to the running hidden state, so the input to layer l+1 is the sum of all prior deltas, not a gated or normalized re-encoding. When adapter N is inserted at layer l and trained, it learns to produce a delta conditioned on the hidden states it sees during task-N training — but those hidden states are themselves the product of whatever adapters exist at layers below l, including adapter N-1 if it sits earlier in the stack. This means adapter N's output is a function of a representational basis that was co-determined by adapter N-1, so the two modules are not geometrically independent even though their parameters don't interact directly. The critical asymmetry is directional: adapter N-1, already frozen by the time task N arrives, cannot update to compensate for the new delta that adapter N injects into the shared stream, so the cumulative hidden state that flows past adapter N-1 on future task-N-1 inference passes now carries an extra residual perturbation it was never trained to handle. Pfeiffer et al. (2021) in the AdapterFusion work implicitly surface this when they show that naively stacking adapters in series degrades individual task performance, motivating their learned attention-weighted combination — the degradation they measure is precisely this cross-adapter residual interference. Concretely, in a 12-layer BERT-base with adapters at every layer, the hidden state at layer 12 is a sum of 12 adapter deltas plus the frozen backbone deltas; each new sequential task adds a new set of those 12 deltas, and the subspace they occupy in ℝ⁷⁶⁸ is under no constraint to be orthogonal to the subspace prior tasks relied on.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1536)
response:
For fusion to provably preserve embedding structure — not just accuracy — the attention weights over adapter outputs would need to satisfy something close to an orthogonal decomposition condition: when processing a task-N-1 input, the fusion mechanism would have to assign zero (or negligible) weight to all adapters trained after N-1, effectively reconstructing the exact residual stream that existed when task N-1's geometry was established. This is a much stronger requirement than recovering classification accuracy, because a linear classifier can achieve high accuracy even on a rotated or rescaled embedding space, whereas geometric properties like inter-cluster distances, neighborhood structure, and manifold curvature are sensitive to any non-isometric transformation of the representation. The fusion attention weights in Pfeiffer et al. are trained discriminatively — optimizing task loss, not a geometry-preserving objective like centered kernel alignment (CKA) or Procrustes distance — so there is no mechanism forcing the weighted combination to be isometric with respect to the original single-adapter embedding. What would be needed formally is that the fusion weight vector w for task k, when applied to the matrix of all adapter outputs, produces a vector in the same affine subspace as the original task-k adapter output alone; this is only guaranteed if adapter outputs from later tasks lie entirely outside the subspace spanned by task-k-relevant directions, which is empirically false in shared-backbone settings where all adapters see the same frozen feature basis. Chronopoulou et al. (2023) and related work on task arithmetic suggest that adapter output vectors across tasks are far from orthogonal in practice — their interference in weight space is linear and measurable — making the zero-weight condition an approximation at best, and an unreliable one as the number of sequential tasks grows. The deeper issue is that fusion's attention is input-conditioned but not subspace-constrained, so it can accidentally suppress a geometrically critical adapter output on ambiguous inputs that don't cleanly activate the task-k attention head.

If you wanted to measure embedding space fragmentation directly — not via downstream task accuracy but via geometry — what specific metric or combination of metrics would be sensitive enough to detect the early-stage degradation before it surfaces in accuracy numbers, and what are the failure modes of each?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1537)
response:
The strongest early-warning metric is centered kernel alignment (CKA), which measures representational similarity between two embedding matrices (e.g., task-N-1 embeddings before and after task-N adapter training) in a way that is invariant to orthogonal transformation and isotropic scaling — Kornblith et al. (2019) show it detects layer-wise representational drift that cross-accuracy comparisons miss entirely. Its failure mode is that CKA is insensitive to anisotropic rescaling: if a new adapter compresses one semantic direction by 0.1x and expands another by 10x, CKA can remain high while neighborhood structure is destroyed, meaning it will miss fragmentation that manifests as variance collapse along task-specific subspace directions. Intrinsic dimensionality estimates (e.g., TwoNN from Facco et al. 2017, or the MLE estimator from Levina & Bickel) catch a different failure mode — when sequential adapters cause the effective manifold to collapse from, say, 40 intrinsic dimensions to 12, retrieval and clustering degrade catastrophically while CKA stays above 0.9 — but intrinsic dimensionality is notoriously noisy on small samples and sensitive to the local neighborhood size parameter. Neighborhood overlap (the fraction of a point's k-nearest neighbors that are preserved across the pre/post-adapter embedding, sometimes called k-NN stability) is the most directly interpretable for retrieval-system failure, and Rajendran et al. and related probing work suggest it degrades measurably after even one sequential task before accuracy drops; its failure mode is that it treats all neighbors equally, so it misses the case where rank order is preserved but metric distances are distorted enough to break threshold-based retrieval. A practical battery would combine CKA (global structure), TwoNN intrinsic dimensionality (manifold integrity), and k-NN stability at k=10 and k=100 (local vs. regional neighborhood preservation), run on a fixed frozen probe set drawn from all prior tasks — the combination catches fragmentation that any single metric masks, though the computational cost of maintaining that probe set without violating the no-rehearsal constraint is itself a non-trivial design problem.

The most principled rehearsal-free approach is to use the frozen backbone's own activation statistics as a proxy for prior task geometry — specifically, storing a compact summary of the residual stream's covariance structure after task-N-1 training (a 768×768 matrix for BERT-base, or its top-k eigenvectors for k≈50) and then monitoring, during task-N adapter training, how much the task-N adapter's output delta projects onto those eigenvectors. If the new adapter's deltas have high cosine similarity with the top eigenvectors of the prior task's residual covariance, it is actively writing into the same subspace that prior tasks used for discrimination, which is a direct geometric fragmentation signal computable from task-N data alone. This idea is adjacent to EWC (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), which uses the Fisher information matrix as a proxy for parameter importance, but the key difference here is operating in activation space rather than parameter space — the Fisher diagonal over adapter parameters doesn't tell you which directions in ℝ⁷⁶⁸ are being corrupted, only which parameters are changing. A more lightweight version would track the spectral norm of the adapter output matrix on task-N minibatches and compare it against the stored spectral norm from task-N-1's final adapter — a sudden increase signals the new adapter is generating deltas of a magnitude that will distort the prior residual scale, detectable mid-training without any prior task examples. The failure mode of the covariance-eigenvector approach is that it requires storing O(d²) or O(d·k) statistics per task, which grows linearly with task count and can itself become a memory burden; the spectral norm proxy is cheap but insensitive to directional fragmentation where norm is preserved but the delta rotates into a damaging subspace.

With k≈50 eigenvectors per task, the union of prior-task subspaces spans all of ℝ⁷⁶⁸ after roughly 768/50 ≈ 16 tasks under the optimistic assumption that each task's top-50 eigenvectors are perfectly orthogonal to all prior tasks — in practice, tasks from related distributions share leading eigenvectors, so effective subspace coverage saturates faster, potentially after 8-10 tasks on benchmarks like Split-CIFAR or standard NLP continual learning suites. Once the union spans ℝ⁷⁶⁸, the fragmentation signal collapses entirely: any new adapter delta, regardless of how damaging it is to prior geometry, will project substantially onto the stored eigenvectors of some prior task, making the projection-based early-warning signal fire as a false positive or become uninterpretable as a task-specific alarm. This is a fundamental detectability ceiling, not an engineering fix — it reflects the fact that a d-dimensional space can only accommodate a finite number of geometrically distinguishable subspaces, and long task sequences inevitably exhaust that capacity. One partial mitigation is to maintain not just eigenvectors but eigenvalue magnitudes as weights, so the alarm is triggered only when a new adapter delta projects onto directions that were high-variance for a specific prior task, not merely directions that appear in its top-50; this preserves some discrimination even when subspaces overlap, but degrades gracefully rather than solving the problem. The deeper implication is that rehearsal-free geometric monitoring has an intrinsic horizon — roughly proportional to d/k — beyond which the embedding space is so thoroughly claimed by prior tasks that fragmentation becomes geometrically indistinguishable from normal adapter operation, which suggests that truly long continual learning sequences may require periodic subspace consolidation steps analogous to sleep-phase memory consolidation in neuroscience, where prior task subspaces are merged and compressed to free geometric capacity.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1540)
response:
Concretely, merging prior-task eigenvector sets without data means operating on the eigenvector matrices themselves — the natural operation is to stack the per-task eigenvector matrices {V₁, V₂, ..., Vₙ} where each Vᵢ ∈ ℝ⁷⁶⁸ˣᵏ, form their union as a tall matrix, and run a second-level SVD to find the top-k directions that best span the union, producing a compressed basis V_merged ∈ ℝ⁷⁶⁸ˣᵏ. This is precisely the incremental PCA setting studied by Ross et al. (2008), and the compression is lossless in one specific sense: the principal angles between V_merged and any individual Vᵢ can be made arbitrarily small by choosing k large enough — but the eigenvalue weights, which encoded how much variance each task placed on each direction, are provably destroyed in the merge unless you also store the per-task eigenvalue spectra separately. What is irrecoverably lost is task-specific anisotropy: if task 3 placed 80% of its residual variance along a single direction and task 7 placed 5% along the same direction, the merged basis treats that direction as generically important without knowing it was critically important to task 3 and incidental to task 7 — so the consolidated subspace can no longer support task-specific fragmentation detection, only aggregate geometric degradation. A second irrecoverable loss is inter-task discriminative geometry: the angles between per-task subspaces encode which tasks are representationally similar, and once subspaces are merged those inter-subspace angles are gone, collapsing information that would have been essential for routing inputs to the correct adapter or detecting task-boundary confusion. Mathematically, the compression maps from a product space of n Grassmannians Gr(k, 768)ⁿ to a single Gr(k, 768), and this map has no inverse — the fiber above any merged subspace contains exponentially many distinct per-task configurations, making reconstruction from the merged basis alone an ill-posed problem regardless of compute budget.

Since eigenvalue anisotropy is provably lost in subspace consolidation, could you instead preserve it by storing a per-task Gaussian approximation — mean and covariance — of the residual stream distribution, and what are the exact conditions under which a Gaussian summary is sufficient versus pathologically misleading as a geometric anchor?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1541)
response:
A per-task Gaussian summary (μᵢ ∈ ℝ⁷⁶⁸, Σᵢ ∈ ℝ⁷⁶⁸ˣ⁷⁶⁸) does preserve eigenvalue anisotropy exactly — the eigenvectors of Σᵢ are the principal directions and the eigenvalues are the per-direction variances, so you recover everything lost in bare subspace consolidation — and the storage cost is dominated by Σᵢ at ~2.4M floats per task for BERT-base, which is roughly 9.4MB per task in float32, manageable for tens of tasks but linearly growing. The Gaussian summary is sufficient as a geometric anchor under two conditions: first, the residual stream distribution for task i is genuinely elliptically symmetric (unimodal, no heavy tails, no multimodal cluster structure), and second, fragmentation manifests as changes to second-order statistics — covariance rotation or eigenvalue rescaling — rather than higher-order structural changes. The first condition fails badly for tasks with multiple semantic classes, where the residual distribution is a mixture of Gaussians with one component per class cluster; a single Gaussian fitted to a 10-class task will have an artificially inflated covariance that smears across inter-class gaps, making it impossible to detect fragmentation that selectively destroys one class cluster's geometry while leaving others intact. Specifically, if a new adapter collapses the residual representations of class 3 and class 7 into the same region while leaving classes 1,2,4-6,8-10 intact, the aggregate Gaussian mean and covariance will shift only slightly — the per-class signal is diluted by the 8 unaffected classes — and the fragmentation will be invisible until it's severe enough to distort the mixture's global moments. The Gaussian summary becomes pathologically misleading when used to compute Fréchet distance (as in FID scores for generative models) between pre- and post-adapter distributions: Fréchet distance assumes Gaussianity explicitly, so a low Fréchet distance after task-N training will be interpreted as geometric preservation when the actual per-class manifold structure has been substantially reorganized within a globally similar covariance envelope. The correct fix is storing per-class Gaussians — one (μᵢc, Σᵢc) per class c per task i — which recovers sensitivity to class-selective fragmentation at the cost of scaling storage with the number of classes, and requires knowing class labels at consolidation time, which is not always guaranteed in continual learning protocols with unlabeled or weakly labeled streams.
